To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ambiguities in Euclidean reconstruction and reprojections can be described by a finite number of subgroups of the projective group.

(1) the reconstruction is ambiguous if the camera is translating in the plane spanned by the first two singular vectors of the motion matrix; (2) for a given reconstruction, the camera calibration is ambiguous if the motion is a pure rotation; (3) for a given calibration, the motion is ambiguous if the calibration is a pure translation; (4) the vantage point is ambiguous if it is on the plane spanned the first two singular values of the motion matrix, and (5

(1) the reconstruction is Euclidean if and only if the camera motion belongs to the group of Euclidean motions; (2) the Euclidean reconstruction and reprojections can be recovered from the reconstruction up to the subgroup of Euclidean motions, and (3) the Euclidean reprojections can be computed from the reconstruction up the subgroup of affine motions.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following question: given a set of images of a scene, what can be estimated about the scene, the motion and the calibration of the camera? Our results are the most comprehensive to date, and we show that they can be used to generate novel views of the 3D scene.
the question: What exactly can be recovered from a sequence of views of a rigid scene that does not satisfy all the conditions for a unique Euclidean reconstruction?
the question of what can be estimated from image data, and how the results can be manipulated.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Euclidean reconstruction and reprojections are invariant under the action of a certain subgroup of the group of all Euclidean transformations.

“Given a sequence of images of a scene, if the camera moves in a way that fails to meet all the conditions for a valid Euclidean reconstruction and reprojections, the scene and motion can be reconstructed up to a subgroup of the Euclidean group, the calibration can be recovered up to a subgroup in the group of projective transformations and the reprojections are up to the same subgroup of the group of projectivities.”

, in the general case, the scene, camera and motion can be recovered up to the action of a subgroup of the Euclidean group, and that, for a given motion, the subgroup can be explicitly computed and used to generate novel views of the reconstructed scene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we give necessary and sufficient conditions on the camera motion for the Euclidean reconstruction to be possible up to any subgroup of SE(3), and that we give the explicit formulas for the ambiguity in the case that the reconstruction fails to be possible up the entire Euclidean group.

, in a sequence of images taken by a camera that moves along a general motion, the Euclidean reconstruction and reprojections can be computed up to the action of the stabilizer of a point on the motion axis.
we give a complete characterization of all the vantage views that can be generated by an arbitrary camera motion, regardless of the scene structure and camera calibration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ambiguities in Euclidean reconstruction and reprojections can be controlled by the vantage point, and that the set of possible vantage points is surprisingly rich.
the ambiguities are not as mysterious as they seem.
the ambiguities in reconstruction are much more subtle than the well known ambiguities in the estimation of the fundamental matrix.
